title: Trader Joe’s Is the Next Sephora
text:
Earlier this year, when Trader Joe’s released a list of the 11 products its customers loved the most, a bright-pink tub of Brazil Nut Body Butter was featured among the potato chips and ice-cream sandwiches. The $6 moisturizing lotion was much cheaper than similar items on the market, the announcement noted. But its fans already knew that it was a close match for the popular $48 Sol de Janeiro Brazilian Bum Bum Cream. The TJ’s lotion had both a similar ingredient list and a similar scent of pistachio, salted caramel, and vanilla (if a less embarrassing name).

 That body butter is just one of the many TJ’s skin-care products that bear a striking resemblance to expensive cult favorites. The $10 vitamin C might stand in for SkinCeuticals’ $185 version. The TJ’s facial sunscreen rubs in as cleanly as a $38 Supergoop formulation. Just as Trader Joe’s snack fanatics have long tried to prove that the grocer uses the same manufacturers as name-brand favorites, people on beauty Subreddits are judging how closely TJ’s beauty offerings mimic the brands they’d find at Sephora.

 Like most grocery stores, Trader Joe’s has sold a limited selection of personal-care items for years. But more recently it has pushed further and further beyond the realm of lotion and tissues to offer skin-care products usually priced at a premium. Dermatologists and beauty publications now take TJ’s seriously as a beauty supplier; influencers (only semi-)joke that it’s “the next Sephora.” Buying Milky Hydrating Bi-Phase Face Mist from a store known for its frozen orange chicken might sound a little weird. But Trader Joe’s was built on what the beauty world calls “dupes,” which, in recent years, beauty consumers have become more primed to accept.

 Since opening its first store in the 1960s, the grocer has perfected this strategy for food. Its aisles are full of products that might remind you of other ones—instead of Oreos, they have Joe-Joe’s; instead of Swedish Fish, they have Scandinavian Swimmers. By outsourcing manufacturing to third parties, then selling the products under its private label, Trader Joe’s can undercut the competition on price. The company declined to provide details on its beauty-manufacturing process, but many beauty companies similarly use contract manufacturers, Alexis Wolfer, a McKinsey partner who’s the head of its North American beauty practice, told me. And over the past five years, those manufacturers have started “giving new or mass brands access to a lot of very similar advanced formulations that once belonged exclusively to the big houses,” she said. They’ve effectively democratized the supply chain to keep up with consumer demand for cheap, high-quality products—in effect matching what Trader Joe’s has been able to do for years with its food offerings.

 In some cases, Trader Joe’s and other skin-care-dupe companies can offer lower prices largely because another company already invested funds into developing the formula, Kelly Dobos, a cosmetic chemist at the University of Cincinnati, told me. About a year after the patent expired on SkinCeuticals’ original C E Ferulic serum—which pioneered a way to stabilize vitamin C, a notoriously fickle cosmetic ingredient—Trader Joe’s launched a similar formulation for $10. A leader of TJ’s beauty and health division said on the company’s podcast that she got the idea to carry a gel moisturizer after trying an expensive name-brand one. She asked one of the company’s suppliers to formulate something similar for cheaper and eventually got the $9 Ultra Hydrating Gel Moisturizer, which people now compare to a $65 formulation from Clinique.

 People now are also generally more willing to believe that a $10 serum can be as good as a $185 one. Dupes have been around for decades, but they took off on social media around 2022 ; by 2023, the obsession had trickled down to the mainstream enough that nearly one in three U.S. adults said they’d intentionally bought a dupe of a premium product. Just because two products have the same ingredient list doesn’t mean they’ll be equally effective, but over the years, the percentage of consumers who told McKinsey they believe that mass-beauty products can be as good as prestige ones has risen and is now at 63 percent. Whereas shoppers used to pick one price level and stick to it—your grandmother who only got her skin care at the department store, for instance—now people are more open to a good product wherever they find it. “There really isn’t the premium-beauty shopper and the mass-beauty shopper anymore,” Wolfer said. One person’s toiletry bag might contain a TJ’s cleanser they love and a $40 face mask from Sephora. Some of this price-point agnosticism is because of inflation. But people are also generally more aware of skin-care ingredients than they used to be and might be more willing to bet that Trader Joe’s $10 vitamin C serum could do its job about as well as the $185 SkinCeuticals version.

 That anyone who is not a dermatologist has an opinion about vitamin C serum is a sign of the “TikTok-ification of beauty,” as Wolfer put it. Beauty influencers and TikTok dermatologists, for instance, have exposed more people to Sephora “shopping haul” videos and the virtues of hyaluronic acid. And a company that wants to feed the beauty-TikTok beast can’t make just one good lotion—it has to make new ones frequently, and maybe throw in a weird ingredient people can try, like Irish sea moss, for good measure. Trader Joe’s is already set up to meet such a constant demand for new stuff (and it does carry a night cream that contains Irish-sea-moss extract).

 The store’s product lineup changes every week, as new products are introduced, Nakia Rohde, a Trader Joe’s spokesperson, told me. That means that the beauty aisle changes a lot as well, gaining at least one new product in October and two so far this month. Each new item doesn’t have to be terribly different from its predecessors—I doubt the company had to go back to the drawing board for its Cinnamon Roll Flavored Lip Mask after launching a vanilla-flavored one. But when one item has run its course on social media and in people’s medicine cabinets, Trader Joe’s is ready to push another on shoppers (most recently, the Espresso & Cream Flavored Lip Mask). “That also means they’ll just cut a product” out of the blue, Mark Gardiner, the author of Build a Brand Like Trader Joe’s , told me—which can motivate shoppers to pick up an extra bottle of that Supergoop-esque sunscreen, in case it’s not there the next time they visit.

 How someone feels about their lip mask or sunscreen—or any product, really—may depend on how much they enjoyed the shopping experience. You could purchase essentially the same body butter at CVS or Sephora or Bloomingdale’s and come away with a very different impression of how much you’d treated yourself. Trader Joe’s has spent decades figuring out how to create the illusion for budget shoppers that they are not budget shopping, Claus Ebster, a marketer who has studied Trader Joe’s, told me. With its Tiki decor, Hawaiian shirts, and vaguely flirtatious cashiers, Trader Joe’s has a more enjoyable vibe than one might expect from a store known for selling a selection of wines for $5 or less. Its store-brand product names, too, try just a little harder than they need to: Midsummer Night’s Cream has a je ne sais quoi to which the Kirkland Signature Body Lotion can only aspire. All of this can create a halo effect around Trader Joe’s products, Gardiner told me. That positive predisposition can be especially important in beauty, when a customer needs to trust a company enough to slather its product on their face.

 Trader Joe’s didn’t provide me with beauty-product sales figures, but the virality of some of these items suggest that at least some people are buying in. Beyond offering similar ingredients, so much of a dupe’s value comes from how well it can replicate the texture, smell, and packaging of a luxury product. But for many younger beauty shoppers, simply being able to own a bunch of products counts as a luxury, Wolfer said. Many women now show off their Trader Joe’s hauls on social media as if they’re Sephora products worth hundreds of dollars. And ultimately, this serves TJ’s well: People seeking luxury-ish moisturizer on a tight budget will have one more reason to come to the store, and maybe pick up a frozen pizza from Italy along with a cheap bottle of wine for a nice night in. No one’s fooling themselves that this is the exact equivalent of ordering a pizza made with D.O.P. mozzarella di Bufala , opening a bottle of Greco di Tufo, and doing a home facial with $800 of La Mer products. But for many people, it’s close enough.
